subject: singing mouse
title: This Mouse Sings 100-Note Songs and Never Talks Over Its Rival

scenes.text: This mouse sings, and it waits its turn.
Alston's singing mouse, from the cloud forests of Costa Rica and Panama. Its song: up to 100 notes in a row, lasting several seconds.
The notes start too high for you to hear, then drop into range, so what you hear sounds like a tiny bird.
Put two males in earshot and they duet. One finishes, the other starts within a fraction of a second. They almost never overlap.
In 2019, researchers in New York found the switch: a patch of the motor cortex. Cool it, and the mouse's timing falls apart.
Human conversation runs on the same split-second turn-taking. A mouse in the clouds may show how speech is timed.

description:
A Central American mouse sings long songs and takes turns like people in conversation.
Alston's singing mouse produces songs of up to about 100 notes, starting in the ultrasonic range and sweeping down into human hearing. Males answer each other with sub-second precision and rarely overlap. A 2019 study in Science from NYU School of Medicine traced this turn-taking to the orofacial motor cortex: cooling that region slowed the songs and disrupted the timing. Researchers study it as a model for how brains time conversation.
Which animal sound would you most want to hear in the wild?
first_comment: The mice sing faster and more often when a rival is close. Which animal do you think has the most human-like way of talking?
